extracted.intended_audience: researchers, evaluators and policymakers interested in gender differences in research performance and academic careers (scientometrics, research evaluation, grant policy)
extracted.subtask_description: A longitudinal bibliometric study design and analytic framework for comparing male and female researchers' productivity, citation impact, and career outcomes, and for assessing whether career differences reflect performance or bias. Emphasizes data collection, indicator selection, normalization, and multivariate modeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: P: Number of publications (full counting)
rubrics_metrics.description: P: Number of publications, full counting
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a basic productivity indicator; size-dependent. Include publications of types article, letter, note, proceedings paper, review. Be aware full counting inflates outputs for multi-author papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frac P: Number of publications (fractional counting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frac P: Number of publications, fractional counting based on author shares
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fractional counting attributes fractional credit to co-authors and is recommended when accounting for co-authorship; authors note committees/panels may implicitly account for co-authorship, so fractional productivity can better reflect perceived contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: NCSf: Field-normalized citation score (full window)
rubrics_metrics.description: NCSf: Field normalized citation score, until 2014
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Field-normalized citation score adjusts for field-specific citation practices. Use equal citation windows where possible; indicators are size-independent and should be interpreted alongside productivity measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: NCSf2y: Field-normalized citation score (2-year window)
rubrics_metrics.description: NCSf2y: Field normalized citation score, 2 years window
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A short-window citation impact measure to capture recent impact; include alongside longer windows to account for citation accumulation differences by publication year.

rubrics_metrics.name: TOP x% indicators: share of publications in top-cited classes
rubrics_metrics.description: TOP x%: Share of publications in the set of (1, 5, 10, 25 and 50 %) highest cited publications, field normalized
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple top-percentile thresholds (top 1%, 5%, 10%, etc.) to identify high-impact output. These are size-independent shares within a researcher’s oeuvre; report several thresholds because effects may differ across cutoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field normalization of citation indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: All citation-based indicators should be field normalized
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Field normalization is critical to compare researchers across fields. The paper stresses using field-normalized indicators to avoid misleading cross-field comparisons and to confirm prior findings when reanalyzing with normalized measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of equal citation windows and multiple citation-window approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations measured with (i) a 3-year window (including publication year) and (ii) without a time window (citations up to end of 2014)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare time-windowed and cumulative citations to account for differential citation accumulation by publication year; include application year/academic age as a confound because older publications have more time to accrue citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual data cleaning and author disambiguation
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication data were manually cleaned by comparing WoS records with authors' publication lists to delete homonyms and add missing items
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manual disambiguation increases dataset reliability for modest sample sizes. Check for different initials, homonyms, and inconsistent first-name formats; automated coupling can leave errors—manual checking is recommended where feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample selection: choose fields well-covered by bibliographic databases
rubrics_metrics.description: Select fields (here: psychology, behavioral & educational research, economics) where the Web of Science covers academic output relatively well
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit bibliometric analyses to disciplines with sufficient WoS coverage or explicitly note coverage limitations; justify field selection relative to the research question and sample representativeness (e.g., applicants to an early-career grant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include application year / academic age as confounding variable
rubrics_metrics.description: Include the application year (reflecting academic age) as a confounding variable because years active affect output and citations
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use academic age to control for time-in-career differences (applications within three years after PhD were used here). Small year differences can substantially affect performance over a 10-year follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use non-parametric statistics for skewed bibliometric data
rubrics_metrics.description: Because bibliometric data are skewed, use non-parametric statistics: compare means, medians, distributions; Mann–Whitney tests; SPSS non-parametric tests and ANOVA alternatives
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test medians and distributions rather than relying solely on parametric assumptions. Report both mean and median ratios (e.g., Male/Female productivity ratio) because skewness can affect means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model career outcomes with appropriate ordinal regression (generalized linear models)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Generalized Linear Models for the ordinal response (multinomial) model with a cumulative logit link function to predict ordinal career level
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the dependent variable is ordinal (e.g., rank codes 10–16), apply ordinal regression (cumulative logit) and include performance, gender, mobility, academic age, and discipline as independent variables. Report model fit (deviance, degrees of freedom) and reference categories for nominal variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure mobility and include it as explanatory variable
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure mobility at three levels: no mobility, national mobility, international mobility
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include mobility because it may influence career progression. Consider not only occurrence of mobility but also quality (institutional ranking, upward vs downward moves) as a refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure discipline and include in models
rubrics_metrics.description: Include discipline (economics, psychology, education & behavior) as an independent variable because labor markets and career dynamics differ by field
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test discipline effects against a reference discipline; interpret differences in career speed and performance in light of disciplinary labor market differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalize career position on an ordinal scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Current position measured on an ordinal scale with values from 10 (teacher) to 16 (full professor) corresponding to university job-structure codes
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map institutional job titles to a numeric ordinal scale to enable statistical modeling of career level; exclude or handle cases who left academia separately, as their positions do not map well onto academic rank codes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for self-selection and representativeness of applicant pools
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether applicants are statistically representative of male and female populations and account for self-selection processes that correlate with performance
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without knowing representativeness, success-rate comparisons can be misleading. Consider that self-selection (e.g., women applying only when stronger) can bias observed success rates and must be accounted for when evaluating bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: measure bias relative to performance differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Bias can only be measured against performance differences; studies that compare success rates without controlling for performance cannot validly claim presence or absence of gender bias
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always combine performance data with outcomes (grant decisions, hiring) to assess whether differences are merit-based or reflect bias. Use bibliometric correlates to grading and ranking procedures where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider topic choice and use field-adjusted productivity indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed productivity differences may be an effect of different topic choice within disciplines; use field-adjusted productivity indicators to test this at a disaggregated level
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If researchers concentrate in subfields with different publication practices, aggregate field normalization may be insufficient—deploy more granular field adjustment or size-dependent indicators as supplemental analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish size-independent vs size-dependent indicators and their interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: Citation-based indicators used here are size-independent and field normalized; size-dependent indicators measure absolute number of top papers rather than shares
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit which class of indicators is used. Size-independent shares (e.g., % top papers) control for oeuvre size; size-dependent measures (absolute counts) reflect total contribution and are sensitive to productivity differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data collection query construction for WoS retrieval
rubrics_metrics.description: Use AU = last_name first–initial* AND (CU = Netherlands OR CU = 'country name') AND DT = (article OR letter OR note OR proceedings paper OR review) AND PY = [years]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include all countries where the researcher has worked according to CV; expect disambiguation issues from homonyms and use manual checks. Consider including non-domestic addresses and expanded indices (SCI-expanded, SSCI, AHCI) for broader coverage.
